title: Max Chunks To Make Sorted II
description: Brute force to optimized: rescanning prefix max and suffix min versus a single pass stack of chunk maximums.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array arr that may contain duplicate values, split it into the maximum possible number of contiguous chunks, such that sorting each chunk individually and concatenating them back together in order produces the fully sorted version of the whole array.

blocks.text: Given an array arr that may contain duplicate values, split it into the maximum possible number of contiguous chunks, such that sorting each chunk individually and concatenating them back together in order produces the fully sorted version of the whole array.

blocks.title: Analogy: Cutting a Shuffled Deck Into the Fewest Safe Piles
blocks.text: Like cutting a partially shuffled deck of numbered cards into as many separate piles as possible, where each pile can be shuffled and sorted entirely on its own without ever needing a card from another pile to end up in the correct final order.

blocks.caption: A valid chunk boundary means everything before it is truly smaller than everything after it

blocks.content: {"headers":["Chunk","Values","Why it is a valid boundary"],"rows":[["Chunk 1","[2, 1]","max of this chunk (2) is less than or equal to every later value"],["Chunk 2","[3]","3 is less than or equal to every later value"],["Chunk 3","[4]","4 is less than or equal to the final 4"],["Chunk 4","[4]","the last element always ends its own chunk"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Every prefix has a maximum (5) larger than every remaining suffix","no boundary before the end is valid","the value 5 sits first but belongs last, so nothing can be safely cut off before it moves there"],["Answer","1 chunk, the whole array","the entire array must be sorted together as a single unit"]]}

blocks.text: Since the array is already fully sorted, every single position is a valid boundary, giving the maximum possible 3 chunks, one per element.
It helps to ask exactly what fact about a boundary makes it safe to cut, and how much of that fact can be tracked without a full rescan.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Sliding Window Maximum just showed that maintaining a monotonic structure, and reacting only when a new value violates it, can replace constantly rescanning the array from scratch.

Observation 2: A candidate boundary is valid exactly when the maximum of everything before it is less than or equal to the minimum of everything after it, so the natural first attempt tracks a running maximum per chunk directly.

Observation 3: A new value that is at least as large as the most recent chunk's maximum can always safely start a brand new chunk of its own, since nothing later needs to be smaller than it. But a new value smaller than that maximum proves the opposite, it actually needed to be sorted inside that earlier chunk, so the two must merge into one.

Observation 4: Keeping a stack of chunk maximums, and merging by popping while the top still exceeds the incoming value, correctly collapses exactly the chunks that must combine, confirmed by tracing arr equal to [2, 1, 3, 4, 4] through to the correct answer, 4 chunks.

Recognizing that a smaller incoming value proves an earlier chunk boundary was invalid, forcing an immediate merge rather than a full backward rescan, is what turns this into a single pass with a stack.

For every candidate boundary position, directly scan the prefix up to that point for its maximum and the suffix after it for its minimum, and the boundary is valid exactly when that prefix maximum is less than or equal to that suffix minimum.

items: For every candidate boundary position i, scan arr[0..i] to find its maximum.
Scan arr[i+1..end] to find its minimum.
If the prefix maximum is less than or equal to the suffix minimum, i is a valid boundary, count it as ending a chunk.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every candidate boundary independently rescans the entire prefix and suffix, so no work is shared between neighboring candidate positions.
The suffix minimum defaults to positive infinity when there is nothing left after position i, correctly treating the very last position as always a valid boundary.
A boundary is only counted when the prefix maximum does not exceed the suffix minimum, directly matching the definition of a safe, independently sortable chunk.

blocks.text: A boundary is valid precisely when nothing before it needs to move past anything after it during a full sort, which is exactly the prefix max versus suffix min comparison being checked here, so this is correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), rescanning the prefix and suffix for every candidate boundary.
Space: O(1), no extra array is used.

Limitation: the prefix maximum and suffix minimum are each recomputed by a full rescan at every single candidate boundary, when the real decision at each position only depends on a small amount of information carried forward from before it.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: rescanning the full suffix for its minimum at every candidate boundary repeats almost the same scan over and over as the boundary shifts by one position at a time.

What tracking chunk maximums as a stack fixes directly: a new value that is at least the most recent chunk's maximum can safely start its own new chunk, needing no suffix scan at all.

What a smaller incoming value reveals: it proves the most recent chunk boundary was actually invalid, since this smaller value needed to be sorted inside that earlier chunk, forcing a merge.

The core idea: maintain a stack of chunk maximums, push a new chunk when safe, and merge by repeatedly popping while the top of the stack still exceeds the incoming value, pushing back a single combined chunk maximum.

Walk through the array left to right while maintaining a stack of chunk maximums built up so far. When the next value is at least as large as the maximum on top of the stack, it can safely start its own brand new chunk, so push it. When the next value is smaller than the top of the stack, it cannot start a new chunk on its own, since it would need to be sorted into an earlier chunk. In that case, merge chunks by popping the stack while its top exceeds the new value, then push a single merged chunk whose maximum is the largest value among everything just popped (which is guaranteed to be at least the new value, since maximums only grow). The final number of entries left on the stack is the answer.
Maintain a stack of chunk maximums, merging chunks by popping whenever a smaller value arrives.

blocks.caption: Optimized: a stack of chunk maximums, merging chunks whenever a smaller value arrives

blocks.text: This works because every entry left on the stack at the end represents one chunk whose maximum never needed to move past any later value, and merging collapses exactly the chunks that a smaller incoming value proves cannot be split apart, so the final stack size is exactly the maximum number of independently sortable chunks.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The incoming value is at least the current top of the stack","It is pushed as the start of a brand new chunk","The chunk count increases by one, since this value never needs to move backward"],["The incoming value is smaller than the current top of the stack","The stack is popped and merged until the top no longer exceeds it, then one combined maximum is pushed back","Exactly the chunks that must combine are merged, and no more"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each value is pushed and popped from the stack at most once overall.
Space: O(n) in the worst case, for the stack of chunk maximums.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Handles Duplicates","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (rescan prefix and suffix)","O(n squared)","O(1)","Yes, but slow","Correct, but does not scale to large arrays."],["Optimized (stack of chunk maximums)","O(n)","O(n)","Yes, and efficiently","The expected answer, the standard monotonic stack pattern for this problem."]]}

blocks.text: This problem is a good test of recognizing when a running maximum comparison needs to be paired with a merge step, since duplicates and out of place small values can force several previously separate chunks to collapse back into one.

items: Applying the simpler running max versus expected running sum trick from this problem's easier sibling (which assumes the array is a permutation of 0 through n minus 1), which silently breaks the moment duplicate values are allowed.
Forgetting to keep merging while the stack top still exceeds the current value, stopping after only a single pop.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["An array that is already sorted","Never needs to merge, and ends with every element as its own chunk."],["An array with many repeated values","Merges can cascade several chunks together at once."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly contrast this with the simpler "Max Chunks to Make Sorted" variant that assumes distinct values 0 through n minus 1, and explain why that trick does not generalize once duplicates are allowed.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "the values can repeat, unlike the simpler version", think: a stack of chunk maximums with a merge step, not the permutation based running sum trick.
If the interviewer says "why does a smaller value force a merge", think: it proves that value needed to be sorted inside the earlier chunk, so the two cannot remain separate.
If the interviewer says "can you do this without extra space", think: in the worst case (strictly decreasing input) the stack can still grow to size n, so O(n) space is unavoidable in general.

items: Why does a value at least as large as the current chunk maximum always safely start a new chunk?
Why must merging continue popping while the stack top still exceeds the incoming value, rather than stopping after one pop?
How does this approach differ from the simpler "Max Chunks to Make Sorted" variant that assumes a permutation of 0 through n minus 1?
How would you also return the actual chunk boundaries, not just their count?
What is the worst case size the stack can reach, and for what kind of input does that happen?
Sliding Window Maximum, whose monotonic deque merging on violation is the same overall shape applied here to a stack of chunk maximums instead.
Any monotonic stack problem (next greater element, largest rectangle in a histogram, and similar), where popping and merging on a violating value is the standard technique.
Prefix and suffix extremum problems throughout this sheet, whose "precompute once, compare directly" instinct underlies the brute force's prefix max versus suffix min check here.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space, using a stack of chunk maximums.

items: Pattern: a monotonic stack of chunk maximums, merging adjacent chunks whenever a smaller value proves the split invalid.

Core Idea: a value at least as large as the current chunk maximum can safely start a new chunk, while a smaller value proves the most recent chunk boundary was invalid and forces a merge, collapsing exactly the chunks that cannot be separated.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach's stack in the worst case.
Most Important Observation: a smaller incoming value is proof, not just a signal, that an earlier chunk boundary was wrong, which is exactly what justifies merging rather than just comparing.

Interview Difficulty: the brute force check is easy to state; correctly implementing the merge-while-popping step, and contrasting it with the simpler permutation based variant, is what shows real depth.
One line memory trick: push a new chunk when safe, merge by popping while the top still exceeds the incoming value.
